exam: A 9‑year‑old boy with short stature has a bone age 3 years behind his chronological age — what investigations and next steps are appropriate? — Assess nutrition, chronic disease, endocrine labs; consider growth hormone trial if labs normal.

A girl presents at 6 years with breast development; hand X‑ray shows bone age 8 years — how does this influence management? — Indicates central precocious puberty; start GnRH analogue, monitor bone age for treatment efficacy.

In a child with known sickle cell disease, bone age is delayed by 2 years. What are likely contributors and how would you address them? — Chronic anemia and marrow expansion; optimise transfusion, treat infections, ensure adequate nutrition.
You only have a dental clinic, no radiology. How can you estimate skeletal maturity for a child with growth delay? — Use dental eruption charts as a rough proxy, acknowledging limited precision.

A refugee child from a malaria‑endemic area has severe malnutrition and delayed bone age. Which reversible factors should you prioritize? — Nutritional rehabilitation, treat any occult infection (malaria, TB), and reassess bone age after 6‑12 months.

Explain why a bone age that matches chronological age does not rule out endocrine disease. — Some endocrine disorders (e.g., mild hypothyroidism) may not affect skeletal maturation early; clinical correlation remains essential.
What are the limitations of the Tanner‑Whitehouse method in low‑resource hospitals? — Requires multiple measurements and scoring sheets; time‑consuming and needs trained personnel, often unavailable.

A child on long‑term glucocorticoids shows bone age delay. How does this affect growth prognosis? — Glucocorticoids suppress GH axis and delay epiphyseal closure, worsening final height; consider tapering dose and endocrine referral.
ai.title: Bone Age Assessment
ai.subject: Paediatrics
ai.summary: Bone age estimates skeletal maturity using radiographs, guiding growth disorder evaluation and endocrine assessment. In low‑resource settings, the Greulich‑Pyle method is most practical.

b: Two main methods: Greulich‑Pyle (atlas) and Tanner‑Whitehouse (score).
sections.p: Bone age compares a child's hand‑wrist X‑ray to standard reference images to determine skeletal maturity. It helps differentiate normal variants from pathologic growth delay or acceleration.

b: Bone age < chronological age → growth delay, chronic illness, endocrine deficiency.
Bone age > chronological age → precocious puberty, hyperthyroidism, congenital adrenal hyperplasia.
sections.p: Skeletal maturity progresses predictably: ossification centers appear, fuse, and epiphyses close. Discrepancy >2 years between bone age and chronological age is clinically significant.

b: Assess growth failure before costly endocrine testing.
Guide timing of puberty‑blocking treatment in precocious puberty.
sections.p: Bone age informs management of short stature, predicts final adult height, and assists in timing of interventions such as growth hormone therapy.

t.b: What is the skeletal maturity? → Matches reference age; discrepancy quantifies delay/advance.
Provides a numeric maturity score when atlas is unavailable or when more precision is needed.
If bone age is markedly delayed, these labs assess endocrine causes; if unavailable, treat based on clinical picture.

b: Growth hormone for proven GH deficiency with delayed bone age.
GnRH analogues for central precocious puberty when bone age is advanced.
Address chronic disease (e.g., treat TB, improve nutrition) to allow catch‑up growth.
sections.p: Treat the underlying cause of abnormal bone age; monitor growth and repeat assessment annually.

b: Dental age uses tooth eruption; useful when hand X‑ray unavailable.
Height age estimates age based on height percentile; less precise.
sections.p: Bone age is not the same as chronological age, height age, or dental age.

b: Late presentation of rickets may show near‑normal bone age.
In severe anemia, bone age may lag despite normal endocrine function.
sections.p: Radiographs may appear normal in early disease; severe malnutrition can cause delayed bone age without endocrine pathology.
